title: The leaf, root hair cells, xylem and phloem

steps.title: A leaf is built for photosynthesis
steps.body:
Cut a leaf across and it is a stack of layers, each doing a job:

- **Waxy cuticle**: transparent and waterproof, so light gets in but water does not escape.
- **Upper epidermis**: a thin, clear protective layer.
- **Palisade mesophyll**: tall cells packed with **chloroplasts**, near the top where the light is strongest. Most photosynthesis happens here.
- **Spongy mesophyll**: rounded cells with **air spaces** between them, so gases can **diffuse** quickly to every cell.
- **Lower epidermis** with **stomata**: pores that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.
- **Veins**: xylem bringing water, phloem taking sugar away.

The leaf is **broad**, for a large surface area to catch light, and **thin**, so gases do not have far to diffuse.

visuals.alt: A cross-section of a leaf with the layers labelled: waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll with air spaces and a vein, lower epidermis with a stoma

check.prompt: Why are palisade cells near the top of the leaf?
check.solution: Chloroplasts need light; the top layer gets the most.
options: That is where the light is strongest, and they hold most of the chloroplasts
That is where the stomata are, so they can take in carbon dioxide first
That is where the veins are, so they can absorb water from the xylem directly
That is furthest from the roots, so they are the last cells to receive water

steps.title: Stomata and guard cells
steps.body: A **stoma** is a gap between two **guard cells**. When the guard cells take in water they swell (become **turgid**) and curve apart, opening the pore. They curve because the inner wall of each guard cell, next to the pore, is thicker and stiffer than the outer wall, so when the cell swells the thin outer wall stretches more and the cell bends away from the pore; when they lose water they go **flaccid** and the pore closes. Open stomata let **carbon dioxide** in for photosynthesis and let **oxygen** and **water vapour** out. Most stomata are on the **lower** surface, which is cooler and shaded, so less water is lost.

visuals.alt: Two stomata side by side: on the left the pair of guard cells is turgid and curved apart, leaving an open pore; on the right the pair is flaccid and pressed together, closing the pore

check.solution: Turgid guard cells bend outwards because their inner walls are thicker than their outer walls.
options: The guard cells take in water, become turgid and curve apart
The guard cells lose water and shrink
Carbon dioxide pushes the guard cells apart
The waxy cuticle melts in the sun

steps.title: Root hair cells
steps.body:
Water and mineral ions enter the plant through **root hair cells** in the roots. Each has a long, thin **hair** that pushes between soil particles, giving a **large surface area**. Water enters by **osmosis** across a **thin wall**. Mineral ions are scarce in soil water, so they are pulled in by **active transport**, which needs energy: root hair cells have **many mitochondria**. They have no chloroplasts, because there is no light underground.

Like other plant cells it has a **nucleus** and a **large permanent vacuole**; what makes it a root hair cell is the hair, the thin wall and the mitochondria.

visuals.alt: A root hair cell with its long extension between soil particles, its nucleus, vacuole and mitochondria labelled

check.prompt: Why do root hair cells have no chloroplasts?
check.solution: Chloroplasts are only useful where there is light.
options: There is no light in the soil, so they cannot photosynthesise
Chloroplasts would block the water entering across the wall
They take in glucose from the soil, so they do not need to make it
They are dead cells, like xylem, so they have no organelles

steps.title: Writing an adaptation answer
steps.body: Adaptation questions are marked as **feature → function** pairs. Name the feature, then say what it lets the cell do, joined by "so".

visuals.problem: Explain how the root hair cell is adapted to its function (3 marks)

steps.text: Long hair, so a large surface area, so more water and ions can be absorbed
Thin wall, so water has only a short distance to cross by osmosis
Many mitochondria, so energy is released for active transport of mineral ions

check.prompt: Which of these is a complete feature-to-function pair?
check.solution: A feature alone, or a function alone, does not score. The mark is for the link, so join them with "so".
options: Thin cell wall, so water has a short distance to cross
Thin cell wall, which is a feature of root hair cells
The cell absorbs water, which is what root hair cells do
Root hair cells are found in the root, near the soil

steps.title: Xylem: water up
steps.body: **Xylem** vessels carry **water and mineral ions** from the roots up to the leaves. They are made from columns of cells that have **died**: the cytoplasm has gone and the **end walls have broken down**, leaving a **hollow tube**. The walls are thickened with **lignin**, which makes them strong and waterproof, so the tube does not collapse as water is pulled up it, and it helps support the plant. Flow is **one way**, upwards.

visuals.alt: A xylem vessel and a phloem sieve tube side by side, with lignin rings, sieve plates and companion cells labelled and arrows showing the direction of flow

check.prompt: Which is a feature of xylem but not phloem?
check.solution: Lignin is the give-away for xylem. Sieve plates and companion cells belong to phloem.
options: Walls strengthened with lignin
Cells that are still living
Sieve plates between cells
Companion cells alongside

steps.title: Phloem: sugar everywhere
steps.body: **Phloem** carries dissolved **sugars**, mainly **sucrose**, from the leaves where they are made to wherever they are needed: growing tips, roots, fruits, and stores. This is **translocation**, and it goes in **both directions**. Phloem sieve tubes are **living** cells joined end to end through **sieve plates**, with **companion cells** alongside. The companion cells have many mitochondria and provide the energy that moves the sugar.

visuals.problem: Why is phloem living but xylem dead?

steps.text: Moving sugar needs energy, so phloem cells need companion cells with mitochondria
Moving water up the xylem uses the pull of transpiration, no energy from the plant
So xylem can be an empty, dead tube, while phloem must stay alive

check.solution: Companion cells are the powerhouse next to each sieve tube.
options: Provide energy for moving sucrose through the phloem
Carry water up from the roots to the leaf cells
Photosynthesise to make the sucrose for the phloem
Strengthen the phloem walls with lignin deposits

steps.title: Your turn: xylem or phloem?
steps.body:
Cover the right-hand column, sort each fact yourself, then check:

| Fact | Tissue |
|---|---|
| Carries water and mineral ions | xylem |
| Carries sucrose | phloem |
| Dead, hollow cells | xylem |
| Sieve plates | phloem |
| Lignin | xylem |
| Flow in both directions | phloem |
| Companion cells | phloem |
| Flow upwards only | xylem |

visuals.problem: A student writes "phloem carries water and sugar up the plant". Correct it.

steps.text: Phloem carries sugar, not water: water goes in the xylem
Phloem flow is in both directions, not just up
So: xylem carries water up; phloem carries sucrose both ways

check.prompt: A tissue has living cells with sieve plates and carries sucrose in both directions. It is
check.solution: Sieve plates and two-way sugar flow: phloem.
options: phloem
xylem
palisade mesophyll
root hair tissue

steps.title: Grade 9: structure to function in a new setting
steps.body:
Top questions give you a plant you have never met and ask you to **explain** or **predict**. The method is always the same: name the structure, name the feature, link it to the function, and say what would happen without it. A desert plant with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata: less evaporation, so it keeps water. Xylem that stayed alive: full of cytoplasm, so water could not flow freely. Companion cells without mitochondria: no energy, so no translocation.

Questions also mix in **magnification** and **surface area** from Key concepts: be ready to calculate magnification = image size ÷ actual size for a root hair cell.

visuals.problem: A water plant has stomata on the upper surface of its floating leaves. Explain why.

steps.text: The lower surface is in the water, so stomata there could not take in carbon dioxide from the air
Stomata on the upper surface are in the air, so gases can be exchanged
Water loss is not a problem for a plant sitting on a pond, so the usual reason for lower-surface stomata does not apply

check.prompt: A plant has xylem with very little lignin. What problem would you predict?
check.solution: Lignin gives strength against the tension of transpiration pull and holds the plant up.
options: The vessels would collapse or burst as water is pulled up under tension, and the plant would be less well supported
Sugar could not be moved down to the roots, because lignin is what pushes sucrose through the phloem tubes
The leaves could not take in carbon dioxide, because lignin is what holds the stomata open in the light
Water could not enter the root hair cells, because lignin is what makes their walls thin and permeable

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Leaf: broad and thin; waxy cuticle stops water loss; palisade cells near the top hold most chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll air spaces let gases diffuse; stomata let CO₂ in and O₂ and water vapour out.
- Stomata open when guard cells are turgid. Most are on the shaded lower surface.
- Root hair cells: large surface area, thin wall, many mitochondria for active transport of mineral ions; water enters by osmosis.
- Xylem: dead, hollow, lignified tubes; water and ions upwards only.
- Phloem: living sieve tubes with companion cells; sucrose in both directions (translocation).

visuals.alt: Xylem and phloem side by side: the xylem a hollow tube with lignin rings and an upward arrow, the phloem a living tube with sieve plates, a companion cell and arrows both ways

questions.prompt: Which layer of the leaf contains the most chloroplasts?
questions.solution: Palisade cells sit just under the upper surface, where the light is, and are packed with chloroplasts.
options: Palisade mesophyll
Spongy mesophyll
Upper epidermis
Lower epidermis

questions.prompt: Name the tiny pores in the lower surface of a leaf that let gases in and out.
questions.solution: Stomata (one stoma). Each is a gap between two guard cells.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the waxy cuticle on a leaf?
questions.solution: The cuticle is a waterproof layer. It is transparent, so light still gets through to the palisade cells beneath.
options: It reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf surface
It absorbs the light energy that the palisade cells use
It lets carbon dioxide diffuse into the leaf more quickly
It carries water from the veins to the palisade cells

questions.prompt: Which tissue carries water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves?
questions.solution: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions upwards. Phloem carries sugars.
options: Xylem
Phloem
Palisade
Epidermis

questions.prompt: Why does the spongy mesophyll have air spaces between its cells?
questions.solution: Gases move by diffusion. Air spaces give a short, fast route between the stomata and every photosynthesising cell.
options: So that carbon dioxide and oxygen can diffuse to and from the cells
To make the leaf lighter so that it can turn towards the light more easily
To store water between the cells for use in dry weather
To hold the chloroplasts in place while the leaf moves in the wind

questions.prompt: Explain how a root hair cell is adapted to absorb water and mineral ions.
questions.solution: Each mark is a feature linked to a function with "so".

criteria.text: The hair gives a large surface area, so more water and ions can be absorbed
The cell wall is thin, giving a short distance for water to cross
Many mitochondria release energy for the active transport of mineral ions against the concentration gradient

questions.modelAnswer: The root hair is a long, thin extension that gives the cell a large surface area, so it can absorb more water and mineral ions from the soil. Its wall is thin, so water only has a short distance to move across by osmosis. The cell has many mitochondria, which release the energy needed to move mineral ions into the cell by active transport, against their concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Xylem vessels have walls strengthened with lignin. Why is this useful?
questions.solution: Water is pulled up the xylem under tension, which would collapse a weak tube. Lignin stops that and helps hold the plant up.
options: Lignin makes the walls strong and waterproof, so the vessels do not collapse and can support the plant
Lignin makes the walls thin and porous, so water can pass through them into the leaf cells more easily
Lignin contains chlorophyll, so the xylem can photosynthesise as water passes up the stem
Lignin lets the xylem cells keep dividing, so the vessels grow longer as the plant gets taller

questions.prompt: Which statement about phloem is correct?
questions.solution: Phloem moves dissolved sugars, mainly sucrose, from the leaves to growing tips, roots and stores, in both directions.
options: It transports sucrose up and down the plant, to wherever it is needed
It transports water upwards from the roots to the leaves only
It is made of dead cells with thick walls and no cytoplasm inside
It carries mineral ions in one direction, from the leaves to the roots

questions.prompt: Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem.
questions.solution: Level-marked. The best answers pair each xylem point with the matching phloem point in the same sentence.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about the two transport tissues, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of the two transport tissues with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of the two transport tissues using the correct terms

criteria.text: Both are tubes running through the root, stem and leaves, formed from columns of cells
Xylem cells are dead and hollow with no end walls; phloem cells are living, with sieve plates between them
Xylem walls are thickened with lignin; phloem tubes have companion cells alongside that supply energy
Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries dissolved sugars, mainly sucrose
Xylem flow is one way, from roots to leaves; phloem flow is both ways, from leaves to wherever sugar is needed
Xylem movement is driven by transpiration; phloem movement (translocation) needs energy from the companion cells

questions.modelAnswer: Xylem and phloem are both continuous tubes made from columns of cells that run through the roots, stem and leaves. Xylem vessels are made of dead cells: the cytoplasm has gone, the end walls have broken down to make a hollow tube, and the walls are thickened with lignin for strength. Phloem sieve tubes are living cells joined end to end through sieve plates, with companion cells alongside that provide energy. Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions in one direction, from the roots to the leaves, driven by transpiration. Phloem carries dissolved sugars, mainly sucrose, in both directions, from the leaves to growing regions and storage organs; this is translocation and it uses energy.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells contain many mitochondria. What is the best explanation?
questions.solution: Water moves by osmosis, which needs no energy. Mineral ions are more concentrated inside the cell than in the soil, so moving them in needs energy.

markScheme.description: Active transport of ions needs energy

options: Mineral ions are taken up by active transport against their concentration gradient, which needs energy from respiration
Water is absorbed by active transport across the thin wall, which needs a large amount of energy from respiration
The mitochondria absorb the light that reaches the root, so the cell can photosynthesise while underground
The mitochondria store the starch made in the leaves, so the root has a supply of glucose for growth

questions.prompt: A plant lives in a hot, dry place. Which leaf adaptation would you expect, and why?
questions.solution: In dry conditions the priority is keeping water. Thicker cuticle and fewer stomata both cut evaporation, at the cost of slower gas exchange.
options: A thicker waxy cuticle and fewer stomata, to reduce water loss
Larger, thinner leaves, to absorb more light
More stomata on the upper surface, to take in more carbon dioxide
No palisade layer, to save water

questions.prompt: Explain why it is an advantage for xylem vessels to be made of dead cells with no end walls.
questions.solution: Structure to function, twice: hollow gives low resistance; no end walls gives a continuous column.

criteria.text: Dead cells have no cytoplasm or organelles, so the vessel is hollow
A hollow tube lets water flow with little resistance
No end walls means a continuous column of water from root to leaf
So water can be pulled up the plant by transpiration in one unbroken stream

questions.modelAnswer: Because the cells are dead, there is no cytoplasm, nucleus or organelles inside, so the vessel is a hollow tube through which water can flow with very little resistance. Because the end walls have broken down, the vessels join into one continuous column from the roots to the leaves. That means the water forms a single unbroken stream, which can be pulled all the way up the plant as water evaporates from the leaves in transpiration.

questions.prompt: A drawing of a root hair cell is 40 mm long. The real cell is 0.5 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Give your answer as a number only, without the × sign.
questions.solution: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 40 ÷ 0.5 = 80. In an exam you would write this as ×80; type just 80 here.

questions.prompt: Most stomata are on the lower surface of a leaf. Suggest why.
questions.solution: Stomata are where water escapes. Keeping most of them out of direct sun reduces the loss while still allowing gas exchange.
options: The lower surface is cooler and shaded, so less water is lost through the stomata by evaporation
The lower surface receives more light, so more carbon dioxide is needed there for photosynthesis
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so it collects under the leaf where the stomata can take it in
The upper surface is covered by the palisade layer, so there is no room for stomata to form there

questions.prompt: By which process do root hair cells take in mineral ions from the very dilute soil water?
questions.solution: The ions are more concentrated inside the cell than in the soil, so they must be moved against the gradient by active transport, using energy from respiration.
accepted: active transport, using energy from respiration

questions.prompt: Why do turgid guard cells curve apart instead of just swelling into a ball?
questions.solution: Uneven wall thickness turns swelling into bending. The thick inner wall hardly stretches; the thin outer wall does, so the cell curves outwards and the pore opens.

markScheme.description: Thicker inner wall, thin outer wall stretches more

options: The inner wall next to the pore is thicker and stiffer, so the thin outer wall stretches more and the cell bends away from the pore
The outer wall next to the leaf surface is thicker, so the cell can only swell inwards towards the pore
The chloroplasts inside the guard cells push against the walls and force the two cells apart
Water enters only at the two ends of each guard cell, so the middle stays the same shape

examTechnique.body: Plant structure questions are almost all "explain how X is adapted to its function". The mark scheme is a list of feature-to-function pairs, so write each one as "feature, so function". For xylem and phloem, comparison questions want matched pairs: dead against living, lignin against sieve plates, water up against sucrose both ways.
examinerErrors: Saying "big surface area" without saying what for.
Mixing up xylem and phloem: water is xylem, sugar is phloem.
Saying phloem carries sugar "up" the plant. It goes both ways.
Saying water enters root hair cells by active transport. Water moves by osmosis; mineral ions need active transport.
Describing the palisade layer as "at the bottom of the leaf".
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer links every feature to a function, applies the same logic to an unfamiliar plant, explains why xylem must be dead and phloem must be alive, keeps osmosis and active transport apart, and can do the magnification arithmetic when it is dropped into a plant question.
